name: Tip plasty / cartilage grafting

image.caption: Nasal tip cartilage suturing during open rhinoplasty

lead: Tip plasty reshapes or supports the end of the nose, using sutures, trimming or cartilage grafts, typically taken from the septum, ear or rib. People use it to refine a bulbous, wide or underprojected tip and get a more defined, better-positioned nose.

It is generally described as one of the more technically demanding parts of rhinoplasty. The surgical literature is extensive but mostly technique descriptions and retrospective series, with a few small trials of specific graft or strut methods.

paras: Surgeons alter the tip cartilages with stitches, add grafts that change contour or projection, or reposition the cartilage, often through an open approach. The new tip shape shows after swelling settles.

A general reference reports that secondary rhinoplasty occurs in roughly 5-20% of operations, and tip or dorsal irregularities are among the reasons. Graft complications, including those of septal extension grafts in Asian patients, have been documented in case series. It is performed by surgeons under anaesthesia.

angle.text: Tip plasty refines a bulbous, drooping or under-projected nasal tip with sutures, cartilage trimming or grafts, and the new tip shape is visible after healing. It is described as a technically demanding part of rhinoplasty. Support comes from technique papers and small trials of specific methods.

lead: Tip plasty (nasal tip refinement) is the part of rhinoplasty that reshapes, repositions or supports the nasal tip, using cartilage sutures, cartilage excision or cartilage grafts. It is generally described as one of the technically more demanding parts of nose surgery.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as the surgical route for a bulbous, wide or underprojected tip. The surgical literature on tip work is large and mostly consists of technique papers and retrospective series; a handful of small registered trials compare specific tip-support techniques.[3][4]

paras: A 1994 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery proposed a systematic approach to primary tip rhinoplasty that favours techniques preserving the structural integrity of the alar rim cartilage strips and limits scoring or morselization, which the authors associated with weaker support and secondary deformity.[1]

Suture techniques have been used for decades; a 2003 history traced the evolution of the main tip sutures,[5] and a 2008 article described five basic sutures (transdomal, interdomal, lateral crural mattress, columella-septal and intercrural) combined in an algorithm to control the shape of tip cartilage.[6] A further review covers suture techniques in rhinoplasty.[7] Older tip operations such as the Goldman tip have also been modified for wide or bulbous lobules.[8]

Grafts are used to add support or change contour. Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article notes that surgeons usually harvest cartilage from the septum first and turn to ear or rib cartilage when more is needed, as often occurs in revision surgery.[9] A review of nasal tip grafts catalogues graft designs, and a 2014 study reported complications of septal extension grafts in Asian patients.[10]

Evidence is mostly retrospective case series and technique papers. Registered trials include a completed phase 4 study of a columellar strut's effect on tip rotation (n=92),[4] a completed study of a new tip-plasty concept in Asian rhinoplasty (n=161),[11] a completed comparison of a septal advancement flap and a columellar strut (n=30),[12] and a recruiting trial of lateral crural steal with columellar strut graft (n=22).[3] Results are not summarised here because they were not reviewed in published form.

timeline.event: A modification of the Goldman tip for wide or bulbous lobules is described.[8]
A systematic approach to tip shaping without structural disruption is published.[1]
The evolution of nasal tip suture techniques is reviewed.[5]
A five-suture algorithm with a universal horizontal mattress suture is described.[6]
